reels.title: The night Ussher said the world began

prediction.prompt: By Ussher's date the world would be about 6,000 years old. How old does radiometric dating make Earth?

frames.text: James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, calculated that the world began at nightfall before 23 October, 4004 BC.
frames.say: James Usher, Archbishop of Armah, calculated that the world began at nightfall before the twenty-third of October, four thousand and four B C.

frames.text: He published the date in 1650, in his Annals of the Old Testament.
frames.say: He published the date in sixteen fifty, in his Annals of the Old Testament.

frames.text: It took real learning: ancient history, astronomy, old calendars and the languages of the Bible.
Where he had several sources beyond the Bible, his dates usually hold up. He put the death of Julius Caesar in 44 BC.
frames.say: Where he had several sources beyond the Bible, his dates usually hold up. He put the death of Julius Caesar in forty-four B C.

frames.text: Radiometric dating puts Earth's age at about 4.54 billion years.

reels.takeaway: Ussher counted back through written records to 4004 BC. Radiometric dating puts Earth's age at about 4.54 billion years.

reels.title: A storm that grew in a day

prediction.prompt: This storm, seen from space on 23 October 2015, set a world record that day. Which one?

choices.label: Strongest sustained winds of any tropical cyclone
Most rain in a single day

frames.text: A storm closes on the Pacific coast of Mexico, photographed by a satellite on 23 October 2015.
frames.say: A storm closes on the Pacific coast of Mexico, photographed by a satellite on 23 October twenty fifteen.

frames.text: This is Hurricane Patricia. In a single day it strengthened from tropical storm to Category 5.
Its sustained winds reached about 345 kilometres an hour, the highest ever reliably measured or estimated in a tropical cyclone.
Near its peak it turned toward land, and weakened fast. It came ashore near Cuixmala, Jalisco, with winds of about 240 kilometres an hour.
frames.say: Near its peak it turned toward land, and weakened fast. It came ashore near Kweesh-mah-la, Ha-lees-ko, with winds of about two hundred and forty kilometres an hour.

frames.text: Mexico's mountains broke it up. Within 24 hours of landfall it was a tropical depression.

reels.takeaway: In about a day and a half Patricia went from tropical storm to the strongest sustained winds reliably measured or estimated in a tropical cyclone, and it faded within a day of landfall.

reels.title: Only a theory

prediction.prompt: When scientists call evolution a theory, what do they mean?

choices.label: A tested explanation of the facts
A fact proved beyond any doubt

frames.text: Evolution is often waved away as only a theory, as if a theory were an opinion or a hunch.
In science the word means something much stronger: a well-supported explanation of the facts.
Before it counts, it must survive repeated tests that try to prove it wrong.
The facts come from fossils that record transitions, from traces of shared ancestry in living things, and from change seen happening now.
That is why many scientists call evolution both a fact and a theory. The evidence for it keeps being tested.

reels.takeaway: In science a theory is not a guess. It is the tested explanation that ties the facts together.

reels.title: Naming the Great Pestilence

prediction.prompt: Medieval England called it the Great Pestilence. How do we know which disease it really was?

choices.label: Doctors at the time named it
DNA from skeletons in a plague cemetery
Rat bones found in old cellars

frames.text: England, 1348. A plague arrives that halts the campaigns of the Hundred Years' War and kills an estimated 40 to 60 percent of the people.
frames.say: England, thirteen forty-eight. A plague arrives that halts the campaigns of the Hundred Years' War and kills an estimated forty to sixty percent of the people.

frames.text: People at the time called it the Great Pestilence or the Great Mortality. The name Black Death came centuries later.
Key proof of what it was came from London, from a cemetery at East Smithfield dug for the Black Death's dead.
In 2011, scientists reported DNA of Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, in skeletons from that cemetery.
frames.say: In twenty eleven, scientists reported DNA of Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium, in skeletons from that cemetery.

frames.text: Its genes showed a strain that was new at the time. Many modern plague strains descend from it.
A new strain probably met bodies with little or no defence against it. That may help explain why so many died.

reels.takeaway: The dead themselves named the killer: DNA from their skeletons showed Yersinia pestis, in a strain new at the time.

reels.title: Whose words were they

prediction.prompt: Who first wrote the phrase "survival of the fittest"?

frames.text: "Survival of the fittest" sounds like Darwin. The words are Herbert Spencer's, from 1864.
frames.say: Survival of the fittest sounds like Darwin. The words are Herbert Spencer's, from eighteen sixty-four.

frames.text: Spencer said his phrase meant what Darwin had called natural selection.
How do we know Darwin borrowed it? His letters. In July 1866 Wallace wrote to him with a worry.
frames.say: How do we know Darwin borrowed it? His letters. In July eighteen sixty-six Wallace wrote to him with a worry.

frames.text: Readers took "natural selection" to mean that nature chooses. Spencer's words, Wallace said, avoided that.
Darwin replied that the phrase's advantages had not occurred to him until that letter. He added it to the fifth edition of On the Origin of Species, in 1869.
frames.say: Darwin replied that the phrase's advantages had not occurred to him until that letter. He added it to the fifth edition of On the Origin of Species, in eighteen sixty-nine.

frames.text: In biology, fittest does not mean strongest. It is best understood as the form that leaves the most copies of itself.

reels.takeaway: Survival of the fittest was Spencer's phrase. Darwin's letters show when and why he borrowed it.
